criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban community/public sanitation service access (public toilets and Community Toilet schemes) across London boroughs for residents with health conditions and gig/delivery workers.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study clearly examines legal, administrative, institutional, and governance factors shaping public toilet access (municipal austerity cuts, fragmented borough governance, and the 'ungoverning' of sanitation). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification, it also qualifies because it empirically examines specific rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access: (1) the absence of a statutory legal duty requiring UK local authorities to provide public toilets (rendering facilities non-statutory in municipal budget allocation), (2) municipal tariff and cost-recovery rules (Westminster's pay-per-use toilet pricing cross-subsidising free-access toilets), (3) administrative design and non-enforcement of Community Toilet (CT) scheme rules (lack of selection criteria/monitoring, participating businesses unlawfully requiring purchases, and discretionary exclusion of marginalised users), and (4) workplace/pandemic legal access documentation and frontline gatekeeper discretion denying toilet access to delivery workers.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative socio-legal and urban-geographical empirical case study drawing on 35 primary interviews (municipal sanitation staff, Transport for London, British Toilet Association, activists/campaigners, unionised delivery drivers, and residents with Crohn's and colitis) plus observation at a Greater London Authority meeting. Per review safeguards, qualitative empirical studies are eligible for mechanism synthesis without quantitative effect estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports outcomes directly relevant to sanitation service availability (closures and borough-level variation in public toilet provision), affordability/cost barriers (pay-per-use charges and forced retail purchases at Community Toilet venues), physical access, and exclusion (gatekeeper denial of toilet access to delivery couriers and marginalised groups, and mobility restriction/'house bound' impacts on residents with chronic illness).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (individuals—delivery workers and residents with Crohn's/colitis in London—and municipal boroughs; n = 35 interviews), rule-type exposures, access/exclusion outcomes, and qualitative case-study design are all clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: Drawing on research in London, we set out the challenges for public toilet provision and make a case for a sanitation revolution in British cities. We focus on the experience of delivery drivers and residents with health concerns in order to illustrate the inequalities in provision and their consequences.
The combination of central government cuts, the lack of legal obligation to provide public toilets, and fragmented state responsibilities has led to an unravelling of provision and responsibility.
She added too that in some CT locations she had been told she had to buy something before using the toilet, which is not how CT schemes are supposed to operate.
We conducted 35 interviews in total, including with municipal staff responsible for sanitation management, local and national activists and campaigners
It has sort of got to the point where I am predominantly house bound. I kind of get sick of all the planning, and all the things that had to go right.

raw_response.exposure: Absence of statutory legal mandate for municipal public toilet provision combined with local authority budget cuts; municipal tariff/cross-subsidy rules (pay-per-use funding free toilets); Community Toilet scheme rules and weak monitoring/enforcement; and workplace/pandemic toilet-access documentation versus discretionary gatekeeping by private premises and security staff.
raw_response.outcome: Public sanitation (toilet) availability across London boroughs, physical and financial access (including pay-per-use fees and forced retail purchases), discretionary exclusion/denial of access for delivery workers and marginalised users, and spatial mobility restriction among residents with health conditions.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban residents with health conditions (Crohn's and colitis), app/supermarket delivery drivers and couriers, municipal borough officials, transport/toilet association staff, and campaigners in London, UK (n = 35 semi-structured interviews plus observation at a Greater London Authority meeting; individual and municipality/borough units of analysis).
raw_response.rationale: This qualitative empirical study of public sanitation in London satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Using 35 interviews and meeting observations, it examines how the non-statutory legal status of municipal public toilets, pay-per-use cross-subsidy tariff structures, poorly monitored Community Toilet rules (including unauthorized purchase requirements), and frontline discretionary gatekeeping despite statutory/pandemic worker-access documentation shape sanitation availability, affordability, and exclusion for delivery workers and residents with chronic health conditions.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative empirical case study (35 semi-structured interviews and institutional meeting observation)
